extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, communications teams, organizations issuing press releases, and journalists who use them
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and distributing press releases: standard structural elements (headline, dateline, intro, body, boilerplate, close), length/paragraph expectations, distribution options (newswire vs self-distribution, video), and embargo etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letterhead or Logo
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include organization letterhead or logo to identify the issuing party and present a professional appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Contact Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Media Contact Information – name, phone number, email address, mailing address, or other contact information for the public relation (PR) or other media relations contact person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least one clear contact (name, phone, email) so journalists can follow up. Omit or redact contacts only when necessary for safety/privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline – used to grab the attention of journalists and briefly summarize the news in one to six words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the headline concise, attention-grabbing, and summary-focused; avoid jargon and misleading claims. The article specifies a 1–6 word target for a quick summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dek (sub-headline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dek – a sub-headline that describes the headline in more detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a short sub-headline to add necessary context or an extra detail that the headline omits; helps editors decide whether to open the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline – contains the release date and usually the originating city of the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include release date and origin city. Note: if the dateline date is after the date the information was sent to media, the sender is requesting a news embargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction (lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction – first paragraph in a press release, that generally gives basic answers to the questions of who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the lead to answer the Five Ws succinctly (who, what, when, where, why). Journalists rely on the intro to produce quick copy; burying essentials is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body
rubrics_metrics.description: Body – further explanation, statistics, background, or other details relevant to the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide supporting facts, quotes, statistics, and background in subsequent paragraphs. Keep language clear and factual; avoid excessive spin. Ensure claims are verifiable since press releases are primary sources for reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: Boilerplate – generally a short "about" section, providing independent background on the issuing company, organization, or individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a concise boilerplate that explains the organization and its mission; keeps release self-contained for editors who need background without further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close (end symbol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Close – in North America, traditionally the symbol "-30-" appears after the boilerplate or body and before the media contact information, indicating to media that the release has ended. A more modern equivalent has been the "###" symbol. In other countries, other means of indicating the end of the release may be used, such as the text "ends".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark the end of the release clearly (e.g., -30- or ### or "ends") so editors know the copy is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and paragraph structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations professionals often follow a standard professional format for press releases. Additional communication methods that journalists employ include pitch letters and media advisories. Generally, a press release body consists of four to five paragraphs with a word limit ranging from 400 to 500. However, press release length varies and can range from 300 to 800 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 4–5 paragraphs and roughly 300–800 words (commonly 400–500). Be succinct; overly long releases waste journalists' time. Adjust length depending on newsworthiness and medium (longer for backgrounders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution model: traditional/newswire
rubrics_metrics.description: In the traditional distribution model, the business, political campaign, or other entity releasing information to the media hires a publicity agency to write and distribute written information to the newswires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broad reach and professional placement, use an agency + newswire. This model scatters information widely but may involve higher cost and less control over placement details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution model: self-distributed press release
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative model is the self-distributed press release. In this approach, press releases are either sent directly to the media or sent via free and paid distribution services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-distribution gives more control and lower cost. Distribution services may provide localized contact lists and deliver content as-is; ensure quality and target the right media to avoid wasted sends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distribution services and media contact lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution services often provide localised, pre-made media contact lists which can be used during distribution. The distribution service then provides the content, as-is, to the selected media outlets for publication via email and online channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vet lists to ensure relevance and update contacts. Avoid mass-blasting irrelevant journalists; targeted outreach yields better pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video news releases (VNRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some public relations firms send out video news releases (VNRs) which are pre-taped video programs or clips that can be aired intact by TV stations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VNRs can include interviews and polished footage; they may cost significantly more to produce. Be aware some broadcast outlets discourage VNRs citing poor public perception. Consider whether VNRs will be viewed as credible and whether they match the outlet's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes and embargo etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: If a (draft or final) press release is distributed in an authorized way before the information is intended to be released to the public it is typically subject to an embargo against publication. An embargo requests that news organizations not report the story until a specified date or time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embargoes to coordinate simultaneous publication. Remember journalists are not legally bound to honor embargoes unless under NDA; breaking an embargo can damage relationships and lead to blacklisting. Share embargoed material only with journalists who have an established relationship and are likely to honor it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat press releases as primary sources; anticipate framing
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release is traditionally composed of nine structural elements... Press releases are also considered a primary source, meaning they are original informants for information. Although using a press release can save a news outlet time and money, it constrains the format and style of its content. In addition, press releases can be favorable towards the organization that commissioned or issued them, framing the topic according to its preferred criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, be transparent and factual because journalists will use releases as primary sources. Avoid excessive spin or promotional framing; provide verifiable facts and independent context to increase credibility and newsroom pickup. Recognize that journalists may need to fact-check or rework prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital-age considerations: speed, editing, and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: In the digital age, consumers generally want to receive information instantly, bringing about pressure on the news media to output information fast with less time for editing and fact-checking. This may cause news media companies to heavily rely on press releases to create stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given rapid publishing cycles, ensure releases are accurate, clear, and ready-to-publish. Mistakes are amplified online; prioritize factual accuracy and clarity to avoid quick propagation of errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending reach: podcasts and community websites
rubrics_metrics.description: Furthermore, VNRs can be turned into podcasts and then posted onto newswires. A story can also be kept running longer by simply engaging "community websites". "Community websites" are monitored and commented on by many journalists and feature writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan post-release amplification (podcasts, community sites, social channels) to extend story life. Tailor assets for each channel rather than recycling the same content unchanged.
